clue.text: His view of Ulysses was singular

definitions.text: His view of Ulysses was singular

parts.words: His view of Ulysses was singular
parts.note: the one-eyed giant of the Odyssey saw Ulysses through a single eye, so his view was singular in the literal sense

explanation.surface: Someone's opinion of the Greek hero was unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'odd', but it means 'through only one eye': the Odyssey's giant had just one.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-eyed giant blinded by Ulysses (Odysseus) in Homer's epic saw him with a single eye.

clue.text: Expert journalist, though crazy

parts.note: crack means first-rate, expert
ED is short for editor, the journalist in charge

explanation.surface: A skilled reporter who is nonetheless unhinged.
explanation.definitionFit: Mad people are informally said to be broken in the head.

clue.text: It's noted to impede steps taken in Holland

definitions.text: It's noted to impede steps taken in Holland

parts.note: to clog is to block or impede
a dance is a set of steps

explanation.surface: Something set to music to hinder footwork done in the Netherlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' means set to music; the whole clue describes a dance in wooden shoes, worn in Holland.
explanation.definitionFit: A folk routine performed in wooden shoes, associated with Holland and northern England.

clue.text: Gay work for a beggar?

parts.note: John Gay wrote a famous musical work named after a beggar in 1728

explanation.surface: A cheerful job offered to a vagrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay' is John Gay, author of The Beggar's ... — the 1728 ballad stage work.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gay's best-known stage work is a ballad drama set to music, named for a beggar.

clue.text: Potential explosive a favourite in arms talks, note

parts.note: SALT is the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks
a pet is a favourite
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A dangerous blast threatened in disarmament negotiations.
explanation.definitionFit: Potassium nitrate is an ingredient of gunpowder, so it is the makings of an explosive.

clue.text: Bloomer made by precise university lecturer, albeit initially

parts.note: prim means prissily precise

indicators.note: initially asks for only the opening letter of the word albeit

explanation.surface: A gaffe committed by a fussy academic, though only at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, but here it is something that blooms: a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A primrose or cowslip is a flowering plant, and anything that flowers can jokingly be called a bloomer.

clue.text: By taking in an aircraftman he sets the rate of progress

definitions.text: he sets the rate of progress

indicators.note: taking in means one piece swallows another

parts.note: per means by, as in per post
AC is the RAF abbreviation for aircraftman

explanation.surface: By recruiting an airman, someone dictates how fast things go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like a link word but supplies PER, Latin for 'by' as in 'per post'; 'taking in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner who leads to set the speed of a race does this.

clue.text: In prison, mostly, financial commitments are underhand

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: inside is slang for in prison
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: Debts run up while in jail are shady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' is British slang for 'in prison'; 'mostly' drops its last letter, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacherous and stealthy means sly or devious.

clue.text: Availing oneself of American gin output

indicators.note: output means the letters of gin are produced in a new form

explanation.surface: Drinking a US-made spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Output' rearranges GIN to ING.
explanation.definitionFit: Making use of something is employing it.

clue.text: Faithful friend's headgear when in the services

indicators.note: when in tells us one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: aces are unreturnable services in tennis
a hat is headgear

explanation.surface: A loyal friend's cap worn while in the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The services' look military but are tennis serves, aces.
explanation.definitionFit: In Virgil's Aeneid this companion of Aeneas is the type of the faithful friend.

clue.text: An advance, say, made by oneself

indicators.note: say signals that the words before it are to be spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: a loan is an advance of money

explanation.surface: A sum lent to someone, made without help from others.
explanation.definitionFit: Being solitary means acting without company or help.

clue.text: Wig-maker, perhaps, providing security?

explanation.surface: A maker of hairpieces who somehow keeps things safe.
explanation.walkthrough: A lock is both a tress of hair and a door fastening, so the first sense is the tradesman read as a maker of hair locks.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as 'one who fashions tresses' it suggests a wig craftsman; really it is the tradesman who fits door fastenings for safety.

clue.text: Does he make off with a youngster taking forty winks?

parts.note: a kid is a young child
forty winks is a short sleep, so someone taking one is a napper

explanation.surface: A question about whether a dozing child-snatcher is at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a question; 'with a' joins it to the wordplay of a sleeping youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: An abductor carries off a person, classically a child, and holds them, often for ransom.

clue.text: Get an eyeful of that figure!

explanation.surface: An admiring remark about someone's shapely figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dig it' is old slang for 'look at that'; 'figure' then shifts from a body shape to a numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Dig it!' is slang urging someone to look, and a single numeral from 0 to 9 is a figure.

clue.text: He was some good in going after a kangaroo

definitions.text: He was some good in going after a kangaroo

indicators.note: some tells us that only a part of the following words, a run of their letters, is wanted

explanation.surface: A wild dog that was rather useful when chasing a kangaroo.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'gooD IN GOing', and the whole clue also describes the animal hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild dog of Australia hunts kangaroos and other marsupials.

clue.text: Old invader of Italy adjusted or got shot

indicators.note: adjusted means the letters of or got shot are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: An ancient raider was either corrected or shot.
explanation.definitionFit: This Germanic people overran Italy in the fifth century.

clue.text: Rita loses materials, but suits us nonetheless

indicators.note: materials are raw stuff to be made into something new, so the letters of Rita loses are remade

explanation.surface: A woman named Rita mislays her fabric, but we are still happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suits us' is a pun: she is the woman who makes suits for us, not someone who pleases us.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman tailor cuts and sews suits for her customers.

clue.text: 'Is it weakness of ——, birdie? I cried" (Gilbert)

definitions.text: 'Is it weakness of ——, birdie? I cried" (Gilbert)

parts.words: 'Is it weakness of ——, birdie? I cried" (Gilbert)
parts.note: the missing word in Gilbert's Tit-Willow song from The Mikado, which asks whether the bird is weak in mind

explanation.surface: A line from a Gilbert and Sullivan song with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from 'Tit-Willow' in The Mikado; the gap is the word for mental power.
explanation.definitionFit: The faculty of reasoning; weakness of it means feeble-mindedness.

clue.text: Ape goes in to ruin Smiley's business

indicators.note: to ruin means the letters of ape goes in are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A monkey comes in and wrecks a cheerful person's firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Smiley is George Smiley, John le Carré's spymaster.
explanation.definitionFit: George Smiley's trade is spying for British intelligence.

clue.text: Candy's a bit near the bone, they say

definitions.text: a bit near the bone, they say

explanation.surface: A sweet that is described as slightly risqué.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense rests on the saying 'the nearer the bone, the sweeter the meat'; 'near the bone' also suggests risqué.
explanation.definitionFit: A sugary confection is candy, and the proverb holds that the meat nearest the bone is the sweetest.

clue.text: Meat product's identified with this island

explanation.surface: A sausage associated with a particular island.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is 'salami is'; the second is the Greek island off Athens, site of a famous sea battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A cured sausage is 'salami is' with the apostrophe; and a Greek island in the Saronic Gulf.

clue.text: Pigment record held in Asia, but capital lacking

indicators.note: held in means one piece is kept inside the other
capital lacking means the word Asia loses its capital, i.e. its first letter

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A colouring disc kept in Asia, although missing its capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital lacking' drops the first A of Asia to leave SIA; 'held in' puts EP inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish-brown colouring originally made from cuttlefish ink.

clue.text: Direct speech

explanation.surface: A plea for plain talking.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct a letter is to write its destination on it, and a formal speech is an oration.

clue.text: Pussyfoot in one game or another

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: loo is an old card game
a pussyfoot was a 1920s nickname for a prohibitionist, after William 'Pussyfoot' Johnson, so a teetotaller, TT

explanation.surface: Treading warily during some game or other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' means another game: a teetotaller (TT) sits inside the card game loo to make a second game.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a game of chance with numbered cards or balls, much like bingo: another game.

clue.text: Drunkard upset about a tragic 3

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a sot is a drunkard
ca is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: A drunk is distressed about a sad event.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' refers to the answer at 3 down, a musical stage work; this one is Puccini's tragic one.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's 1900 work about a singer ends with her leap to her death: a tragic musical drama.

clue.text: Lie about spurious item of academic dress

parts.note: false means spurious or fake
a hood is worn with an academic gown

explanation.surface: A fib concerning a fake piece of graduation costume.
explanation.definitionFit: An untruth is a statement that is not true.

clue.text: Tuck possibly found in the chip shop, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear signals that a word is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: a fryer is the deep-frying vessel or cook in a chip shop

explanation.surface: A tuck-shop treat on sale at the local fish and chip shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Tuck is Robin Hood's companion; a chip shop is a British fish-and-chip takeaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck is an example of a monk of a mendicant order, Robin Hood's merry companion.

clue.text: As a church officer 'e detained the girl

parts.note: held means detained; spoken by an h-dropping speaker, it becomes 'eld
her is the girl; dropping its h as 'e does gives 'er

explanation.surface: In his role as churchwarden, someone kept a young woman back.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''e' tells us the speaker drops his h's, so 'held her' becomes 'ELD 'ER.
explanation.definitionFit: In Presbyterian churches, a lay leader is one of the governing officials.

clue.text: USSR capitalist?

parts.note: a capitalist in the Soviet Union sounds absurd, but here it means someone who lives in the capital

explanation.surface: A free-marketeer in the Soviet Union, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capitalist' here is a resident of the capital, not a believer in markets.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Soviet capital city is a citizen of Moscow.

clue.text: Admiral who died a roué?

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died in genealogies
a rake is a dissolute man, a roué

explanation.surface: Was a famous naval officer a libertine at his death?
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake was the Elizabethan admiral who fought the Spanish Armada.

clue.text: Voluptuous girl unwelcome in a china shop

explanation.surface: An attractive woman nobody wants among the porcelain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smasher' was British slang for a very attractive person; it also literally means one who breaks things.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a stunning person, and literally someone who breaks crockery.

clue.text: Jack attains objectives

parts.note: Jack, as in Jack tar, is a sailor, a tar
gets means attains or obtains

explanation.surface: A man called Jack reaches his goals.
explanation.definitionFit: Goals aimed at are aims or marks to hit.
